sum: AT&T, Inc.T has declined 11.8% over the past year against the Wireless National industry’s growth of 95%. The stock has underperformed the Zacks Computer & Technology sector and the S&P 500’s growth during this period.
T outperform its peers like T-MobileTMUS but underperformed VerizonVZ. T-Mobile declined 20.1% while Verizon gained 15.8% during this time period.

AT&T is benefiting from its aggressive fiber network expansion and improving wireless operations. During the third quarter, the company added a record 769,000 consumer and business Internet connections, comprising 442,000 fiber and 327,000 fixed wireless connections. It also gained 379,000 postpaid phone subscribers, while postpaid phone churn stood at 0.92%.

The company's Advanced Connectivity segment generated $29.48 billion in revenues, up 7.2% year over year. Service revenues increased 6.1% to $23.9 billion, supported by higher wireless subscriptions and broadband demand. Advanced home Internet revenues jumped 23.4% to $2.98 billion, reflecting customer additions and contributions from the acquired Lumen fiber business.

AT&T is also making steady progress in its convergence strategy, which focuses on providing wireless and broadband services to the same households. The advanced home Internet convergence rate improved to 42.8% from 42.5% in the preceding quarter. Its converged customer base expanded by approximately 350,000 during the third quarter. Such bundled relationships can strengthen customer loyalty and support recurring service revenues over time.

The acquisition of Lumen's mass-market fiber business and continued infrastructure deployment have strengthened AT&T's broadband footprint. The company reached approximately 39.7 million fiber locations by the end of the third quarter. It remains on track to surpass 40 million locations by the end of 2026 and more than 60 million by 2030. A larger fiber network offers opportunities to attract broadband subscribers and cross-sell wireless services.
AT&T's enterprise connectivity business is another growth avenue. Business fiber and advanced connectivity revenues increased 8.7% year over year to $1.99 billion in the third quarter.

AT&T stock outlook rises as fiber and wireless growth accelerates
sum: AT&T raised its 2026 adjusted earnings outlook after reporting stronger operating momentum in the third quarter on October 21. The company added record internet connections across fiber and fixed wireless while continuing to expand its wireless customer base. AT&T's third-quarter earnings release said adjusted earnings per share reached 0.65 US dollars, compared with 0.54 US dollars a year earlier.

Revenue rose 5.3 percent year over year to 32.3 billion US dollars. Advanced Connectivity service revenue increased 6.1 percent to 23.9 billion US dollars, while adjusted EBITDA grew 5.4 percent to 12.5 billion US dollars. The reported net income figures were affected by a 2.6 billion US dollar non-cash impairment charge related to the held-for-sale Mexico wireless business and employee separation costs, making the adjusted figures more relevant for the operating comparison.

AT&T added 769,000 consumer and business Advanced Connectivity internet connections, its strongest quarterly result for the measure. Fiber accounted for 442,000 additions and fixed wireless for 327,000. The company also added 379,000 postpaid phone customers, with postpaid phone churn at 0.92 percent.

More than 39 million consumer and business locations were within AT&T's fiber footprint at quarter-end. Management said the company remains on track to exceed 40 million fiber locations by the end of 2026 and more than 60 million by the end of 2030. AT&T also said 42.8 percent of households with its advanced home internet services used its wireless service, highlighting the strategic role of bundled customer relationships.

Chief Executive John Stankey said the company was growing customer relationships as households and businesses adopted AT&T's internet and wireless services together. The company added approximately 350,000 converged relationships during the quarter. That strategy supports subscriber growth, although AT&T said promotional discounts and recently acquired fiber customers continued to pressure fiber average revenue per user.
AT&T now expects 2026 adjusted earnings per share in the 2.40 US dollar range, compared with its earlier outlook of 2.25 to 2.35 US dollars.

Why Did T-Mobile Stock Jump?
sum: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

T-Mobile US (TMUS) shares gained 6.2% on Friday, October 30, 2026, while the S&P 500 lost 1.8%. The company released no announcements, earnings reports, or filings that day. A news report linked the gain to fresh estimates of what it could cost SpaceX to build a rival U.S. mobile carrier. Why would SpaceX’s plans matter to T-Mobile?

SpaceX is weighing an entry into the U.S. mobile market where T-Mobile operates. That potential entry has hung over wireless stocks, one article said on October 30. Another article that day said higher cost estimates for the project were lifting the carriers SpaceX hopes to challenge, with T-Mobile among them.
T-Mobile has already ruled out one way in. On its October 28 earnings call, management said it sees no room for SpaceX to run a mobile service on T-Mobile’s network.

SpaceX would compete for the customers T-Mobile counted in that day’s report. During the third quarter of 2026, the company added 274,000 postpaid accounts. Management calls these monthly-bill customers the all-important part of its business, and its postpaid service revenue grew 9% from a year earlier. The shares slipped 0.5% in the session after that report.

T-Mobile moved with its peers and against the market. AT&T, Verizon, Comcast, Charter and Telephone and Data Systems, the companies on its Trefis peer list, all rose in the same session, with Comcast up 4.3% and AT&T up 2.3%. The SPDR fund that tracks its sector, communication services, fell 1.3%.

No session in the prior 365 days brought T-Mobile a rise this large. The latest big move went the other way: a 7.7% fall on October 23, which left the shares at $146.54, their lowest close of the past year. That fall came after a report that SpaceX was seeking at least 80,000 U.S. cell sites to build a rival carrier.

sum: AT&T Inc. (NYSE:T) is down about 10% over the past year. It is one of the top stock picks in President Donald Trump's latest stock portfolio. Let's see whether the stock can rebound.

AT&T keeps customers longer when they bundle its fiber internet with its wireless service, and 42.5% of its advanced home internet customers already take both. Management says these customers stay longer and spend more, and it targets a 50% rate. The company plans to reach more than 60 million fiber locations by 2030. Its purchase of Lumen's consumer fiber business added more than 4 million locations where only about 25% of homes are customers, against about 40% in AT&T's own footprint. Management explained why bundled customers stay longer on its first-quarter earnings call. Click to read the call transcript here. AT&T is also retiring its copper network to cut costs and raised its 2026 buyback plan.

AT&T spends heavily to build fiber, and its debt is rising. After the EchoStar spectrum purchase, management expects leverage to climb from 2.68 times EBITDA to about 3.2 times before it falls back. Satellite companies are the larger worry, and they explain much of the drop in the stock. SpaceX and Amazon's Leo are pushing into broadband and mobile service, and Oppenheimer downgraded AT&T in June, saying satellite broadband puts its subscriber growth at risk. Carillon Eagle Growth & Income Fund said in its investor letter that AT&T lagged because investors fear a new competitor. Click to read their reasons here. Higher interest rates also make the dividend less attractive and raise debt costs, and AT&T has held its quarterly dividend flat since 2022.

AT&T trades at a forward P/E of 10.02, below the sector median of 12.75 and the market's 19.1, and just above its own five-year average of 9.19. Analyst consensus has earnings per share growing 10.31% in 2026 and 9.92% in 2027, close to the market's long-run rate of about 10%. Revenue is forecast to grow only 2.83% and 2.23%, so cost cuts, lower depreciation and buybacks drive the earnings growth. Management guides to double-digit adjusted EPS growth through 2028. Growth slows in the fourth quarter, with analysts expecting just 1.58%, partly because interest costs rise after the EchoStar deal.

sum: AT&T (T -0.23%), a wireless and fiber connectivity giant, closed at $22.17, down 9.81%. Space Exploration Technologies' spectrum deal raised competitive concerns for legacy wireless providers, and investors are watching Q3 earnings for guidance and subscriber trends.
Trading volume reached 140.3M shares, coming in about 182% above its three-month average of 49.8M shares.

The S&P 500 closed at 7,811, up 0.59%, and the Nasdaq Composite ended the trading session at 27,366, up 0.64%. Among integrated telecommunications services: wireless, fiber broadband, and enterprise connectivity peers, Verizon Communications (VZ +0.42%) closed at $41.65, down 8.75%, and T-Mobile US (TMUS -3.58%) closed at $148.58, down 13.27%, as sector rivals also absorbed the SpaceX spectrum news.
The news from SpaceX hit AT&T and the other communication stocks hard because it undermined one critical pillar of their investment cases — the competitive landscape.

Before SpaceX acquired this spectrum, investors perceived these three telcos as an oligopoly. These companies spend tens of billions of dollars every year to update and maintain their wireless networks. That cost and the prospect of low returns for a new market entrant made it unlikely that additional companies would try to compete in this space.

Now with SpaceX possibly on track to become America's fourth wireless carrier, that investment thesis no longer applies. Moreover, SpaceX could combine its satellite connectivity with a terrestrial wireless network, providing a level of rural coverage that might be cost-prohibitive for the legacy carriers.

However, the decline might be a buying opportunity for AT&T stock. Its revenue and net income continue to grow, and the company generates sufficient free cash flow to maintain its $1.11-per-share annual dividend, which yields about 5%. That cash return and its P/E ratio of 7 might prompt more investors to buy the stock.

What Does AT&T Stock Do To Your Money When The Market Falls?
sum: AT&T (T) is up 4.4% over the last five trading days, while the S&P 500 is down 1.1%. Strength in a weak tape pulls money in. That five-day move is not the question. The question is what holding AT&T does to your money when the market moves, because over the past year it has tended to go the other way.

On days the S&P 500 fell over the past year, AT&T moved about 55% of the index’s move in the opposite direction, so it tended to rise when the market fell. On the market’s up days, it moved about 50% of the index’s move the other way and tended to fall. That is a cushion on the bad days and a drag on the good ones, and a one-year reading can shift.

The ride is not quiet. Over the past five years, AT&T ran 24.7% annualized volatility against 17.2% for the S&P 500. Across those five years the link between the two was weakly positive. AT&T’s daily moves had a correlation of only 0.17 with the index, so most of that swing is its own.

That is a slow business, and the market prices it as one. Revenue over the trailing twelve months grew 2.6% against 8.3% for the median S&P 500 company, and the stock trades at 8.6 times earnings against a median of 22.5.

Most of the free cash AT&T generates goes back out. Management expects to return about $18 billion to shareholders in 2026 through dividends and buybacks, essentially all of the free cash flow it expects for the year.

Not quite. Over the past five years, AT&T returned 11.2% a year against 12.7% for the S&P 500, with more volatility. What you got instead was a return on its own schedule across those five years and, over the past year, a holding that tended to rise when the index fell.

Still a difficult question, isn’t it? And it is the one you cannot answer unless you look at the rest of your portfolio. Is the stock adding to your portfolio risk or reducing it? What about returns? Is there a better alternative?

Does AT&T Stock Actually Diversify Your Portfolio?
sum: Its five-year correlation to the index is low enough that most of its return has been its own story, and over the past year it has tended to move opposite the market.

AT&T (T) stock was up nearly 11% over the course of a week before correcting nearly 3% yesterday. On the other hand, S&P 500 is down over the same stretch, a window that also takes in AT&T’s June-quarter results. A holding that rises while the index falls is tempting, but one week of prices proves nothing about how a stock behaves. The question that decides what this position does to your money is how much of its return is genuinely its own rather than the market you already own through an index fund and what it does to the swings in everything else.

Over the past five years AT&T stock has carried a correlation to the S&P 500 of 0.18. A reading of 1.0 would mean perfect lockstep with the index; 0 would mean unrelated moves. At 0.18, most of what these shares have done has been their own story, which is the defining trait of a genuine portfolio diversifier. It compounded while doing it, at 9.2% a year over that five-year window against 12.7% for the S&P 500, and at an annualized volatility of 25% versus 17.1% for the index. Over those same five years the two assets people reach for instead did this: gold returned 17.0% a year at a correlation to AT&T of just 0.03, while the VNQ real estate index returned 2.9% at a correlation of 0.34. Gold did better on both counts over that stretch; the point is that this stock is a third, largely independent return stream, not a substitute for either.
AT&T Fell On The Market’s Good Days And Rose On Its Bad Ones

The capture readings show how that independence feels. Over the past year, for every move up in the S&P 500, AT&T moved about 51% in the opposite direction, tending to fall when the market rose. For every move down in the index, it moved about 55% in the opposite direction, tending to rise. That is counter-cyclical behavior, not a quiet stock: it leans against the market rather than sitting still through it. The stock has fallen more than 10% over the past twelve months and sits about > 15% below its 52-week high. This is a one-year reading, and it can shift; behind it is a business mid-transition.

sum: AT&T released its second-quarter earnings report on July 22. Here’s Morningstar’s take on AT&T’s earnings and stock.

AT&T’s service revenue increased 2.7% in the second quarter, or about 2% excluding the Lumen fiber acquisition. This was the fastest pace in three years, driven by a jump in revenue per wireless customer. Adjusted EBITDA increased 5%, but management maintained full-year expectations at 3%-4% growth.

Why it matters: Competitive intensity in the wireless business appears to be easing. AT&T increased prices in April, but the pace of customer defections, or churn, was roughly flat with a year ago, and the firm added more net postpaid phone customers than a year ago (432,000 versus 401,000).

- Revenue per postpaid phone customer jumped nearly 3% versus the prior quarter to $58 after being stuck at or below $57 for two years. We suspect the allocation of bundle discounts between wireless and broadband partially drove this result.

- Still, with T-Mobile increasing prices on older rate plans in June, the industry seems to be retreating from the promotional intensity of the past 18 months. Residential broadband customer additions were also strong, especially on the fiber network, as AT&T drives bundle penetration.

Long view: Management forcefully reiterated that it has no interest in selling wholesale network capacity to SpaceX. AT&T expects to fill wireless coverage gaps through its partnership with AST SpaceMobile.
The bottom line: We maintain our $27 fair value estimate for narrow-moat AT&T. Telecom valuations have been under pressure, likely caused by enthusiasm around the SpaceX IPO.

items.t: AT&T Stock Outlook Hinges on Fiber Growth and Wireless Risks in 2026
sum: AT&T Inc. T is trying to show that a cleaner connectivity model can still produce steady growth. The stock story now rests less on media optionality and more on execution in fiber, 5G and bundled Internet-wireless services.

That focus gives investors a clearer operating thesis. It also leaves T exposed to promotional wireless competition, legacy copper declines and the capital intensity needed to keep expanding network reach.
AT&T has moved away from a broader media and video structure. The divestiture of media assets and the sale of its Video business sharpened the company's focus on core connectivity services.

Effective first-quarter 2026, the company realigned reporting around Advanced Connectivity, Legacy and Latin America. Advanced Connectivity generated about 90% of operating revenues in that quarter and now houses domestic 5G, fiber-based wireless, advanced home Internet, business fiber and related services.

The growth case starts with customer additions. In second-quarter 2026, AT&T reported more than 1 million Advanced Connectivity net additions, including 646,000 Internet net additions and 432,000 postpaid phone net additions.

Fiber remained central to that momentum, with 367,000 net additions. Fixed wireless added 279,000 customers, while advanced home Internet connections rose 29.5% year over year. Convergence is another lever. About 42.5% of advanced home Internet customers also had an AT&T postpaid wireless plan, and management has indicated that converged households churn at roughly half the rate of standalone accounts.

AT&T is also positioning the network for heavier edge and artificial intelligence-related traffic. Dense fiber, 5G backhaul and spectrum depth are expected to support lower-latency workloads and stronger uplink performance over time.

Does AT&T Stock Follow Its Own Path?
sum: The telecom giant is standing out in a down market, but its real value for your portfolio is a story told over years, not days.
AT&T (T) stock is having a good week when most are not. Over the last five trading days, it has climbed 1.9% even as the S&P 500 index slid 1.0%. In a sea of red, that kind of green gets noticed.
The immediate urge is to chase what’s working. You see a stock holding its ground while the market falls, and you think, That’s my safe harbor. I should buy more.

But building wealth isn’t about guessing next week’s winner. The more important question for your portfolio is what a stock like AT&T actually adds to the mix. How much of its performance is a genuinely different story, and how much is just another version of the market risk you already own?

Looking at the long-term data, AT&T’s stock price moves to a rhythm largely its own. Its five-year correlation to the S&P 500 is just 0.18. A reading of 1.0 would mean it moves in lockstep with the market; at 0.18, most of its performance has been driven by its own business, not the market’s daily tides. For an investor who already owns an index fund, that’s an attractive profile, adding a return stream that isn’t just more of the same.

The stock’s behavior over the past year has been even more distinct. On days the S&P 500 rose, AT&T actually tended to fall, moving about 59% in the opposite direction. On days the market fell, the stock tended to rise, capturing about 48% of the market’s loss as a gain. This is a one-year snapshot, not a permanent feature, but it shows a stock that has recently provided a powerful counter-balance, zigging when the broader market zagged.

This diversifying behavior is backed by a business in the middle of a strategic overhaul. The company’s big push is “convergence,” getting customers to buy both its fiber internet and wireless services. Management believes this is “the best way for us to manage churn.”
